> Review Board, and participants provided informed consent for research use of their data.

> For the significant candidate proteins, additional IVW MR analyses restricted to European-ancestry participants were performed.

> Colocalization analyses in European-ancestry participants were performed to evaluate whether a shared causal variant within the cis-regulatory region drives the associations with both plasma protein levels and breast cancer risk.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: The plasma proteome may help connect inherited breast cancer susceptibility to biologically interpretable and potentially actionable pathways, but proteome-wide evidence across ancestries remains limited.

Methods: We conducted proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses of breast cancer risk using cis-protein quantitative trait loci for 1,962 distinct plasma proteins from 34,557 European-ancestry participants in the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project.
Breast cancer genome-wide association studies included 156,901 cases and 204,634 controls of European, East Asian, and African ancestries.
Ancestryspecific MR estimates were combined by fixed-effects meta-analysis.

Candidate proteins were further evaluated through subtype-specific and reverse-direction MR analyses, statistical colocalization, replication in independent European and East Asian proteomic datasets, and analyses of associations between protein polygenic scores and breast cancer status in All of Us.
Results: Twelve proteins achieved Bonferroni significance in the cross-ancestry metaanalysis (P < 0.05/1,971 tests), including eight previously reported proteins and four newly prioritized by MR.

Identifying the molecular mediators of breast cancer susceptibility across populations remains a central challenge in cancer biology.

Although genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified over 230 genetic loci associated with breast cancer risk [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] , most risk-associated variants lie in noncoding regions, and their downstream effector mechanisms remain largely unknown 9 .

text.text: We combined ancestry-specific MR estimates through fixedeffects meta-analysis and prioritized 12 candidate proteins associated with overall breast cancer risk.

We then evaluated subtype-specific and reverse-direction associations and assessed robustness through a multi-tiered validation framework incorporating statistical colocalization, replication in independent European and East Asian pQTL resources 36, 37 , and phenotype-linked genetic validation using protein polygenic scores (PGS) in the ancestrally diverse All of Us cohort (AoU, n = 224,107) 38.

Primary two-sample MR analyses paired European-ancestry UKB-PPP cis-pQTL associations for plasma proteins with ancestry-specific breast cancer GWAS associations from European-, East Asian-, and African-ancestry participants.
Ancestryspecific MR estimates were subsequently combined via fixed-effects meta-analysis to generate cross-ancestry effect estimates.
Fixed-effects meta-analysis was used as the primary discovery framework to test for a non-zero pooled association, while Cochran's Q statistic was used to test for cross-ancestry heterogeneity.

Candidate proteins that reached proteome-wide significance (defined as P < 0.05/1,971, where 1,971 is the number of primary tests) in the cross-ancestry meta-analysis and showed robustness across alternative MR estimators and instrument-selection thresholds were carried forward for downstream analyses (Figure 1).

MR estimates were interpreted under three core IV conditions.
Relevance requires that the selected cis-pQTL instruments are strongly associated with plasma protein levels.
Independence requires that the association between the instruments and breast cancer is not confounded, for example, by population stratification or other unmeasured factors.
Exclusion restriction requires that the instruments influence breast cancer only through the target protein, and not through other, independent pathways (horizontal pleiotropy).

We evaluated the plausibility of these assumptions via strict instrument-selection criteria, alternative MR estimators that relax different assumptions about pleiotropy, and additional complementary analyses including colocalization.
These analyses, however, cannot establish instrument validity or exclude residual pleiotropy.
Throughout the forward MR analyses, odds ratios (ORs) represent breast cancer odds per 1-SD increase in genetically predicted plasma protein levels.
We use "risk" to refer to breast cancer susceptibility.

Only variants present in both datasets were retained.

The 12 candidate proteins differed in the extent of primary MR analysis, strong colocalization, and at least one external replication or phenotype-linked validation result.
CASP8 and DNPH1 showed strong primary MR and colocalization corroboration, although external support was limited for CASP8 and interpretation of DNPH1 is complicated by cross-ancestry heterogeneity.
RALB, GCLM, SCAMP3, RSPO3 and USP28 were supported by the primary MR analysis together with at least one additional validation layer, but lacked strong colocalization evidence.
ADM and ANXA4 should be considered more provisional: ADM had limited support across validation analyses, whereas ANXA4 showed platform-dependent directional inconsistency.

This proteome-wide MR study identifies 12 plasma proteins associated with breast cancer risk and shows that support for these associations varies across ancestryspecific, subtype-specific, and validation analyses.

By combining cross-ancestry MR with colocalization, external proteomic replication, and phenotype-linked genetic validation, we prioritized a subset of candidates with stronger cumulative evidence for involvement in breast cancer susceptibility.
Collectively, these findings nominate genetically prioritized plasma proteins for mechanistic investigation and translational follow-up.
Our findings both reinforce prior work and extend it.

Among our 12 candidate proteins, eight had previously been linked to breast cancer risk by MR, all concordant in direction with the reported significant associations in those studies 23, [25] [26] [27] [28] [29] .

text.text: Associations with other conditions do not preclude a role in breast cancer etiology, provided the pathways these proteins act through are active in breast tissue, through local and/or systemic effects.
How these tissue-level functions relate to genetically predicted circulating levels, however, remains unresolved.
A notable finding was the directionally heterogeneous association of DNPH1 across ancestries.

This pattern could reflect true biological heterogeneity, but it could also arise from imperfect transferability of European-derived instruments to non-European populations, given ancestry differences in LD structure, allele frequency, and regulatory architecture.
Complementary analyses across East Asian UKB-PPP and JCTF pQTL datasets suggested that the directional difference is not fully explained by European-derived effect estimates alone.

Biologically, DNPH1 has been linked to sensitivity to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibition in BRCA1/2-deficient cells 64 , and population differences in BRCA founder mutations 65 suggest a possible source of variation in its biological relevance, although this explanation remains speculative.

Several limitations warrant consideration.
Our primary instruments were derived from European-ancestry participants because comparably large non-European pQTL resources are not yet available.

text.text: Ancestry classifications were also source-defined and not uniformly harmonized across datasets, and broad ancestry labels obscure within-group diversity, which could not be assessed from the available pooled summary statistics.
Subtype-stratified analyses were restricted to Europeanancestry data, and the smaller case counts for several subtypes limit statistical power for detecting subtype-specific associations.
The shared-control adjustment used a covariance approximation because covariance matrices from the fitted subtype GWAS model were unavailable.
We did not directly assess whether genetic effects on protein levels vary with age.
If they do, the cis-pQTL weights estimated in the exposure sample may not fully transport to the outcome populations, potentially biasing the MR estimates.
Sex-combined pQTL estimates were used in the primary analyses to maximize exposure sample size and instrument availability.

The high concordance between the female-only and sex-combined estimates supports the robustness of the evaluated associations, although the smaller female-only sample and incomplete instrument coverage limit power to assess sex-specific effects.

Restricting instruments to cis-pQTLs mitigates concerns about horizontal pleiotropy, but, even with our alternative MR analyses, does not exclude effects on breast cancer through pathways independent of the target protein.

This cross-ancestry proteome-wide MR study identified 12 plasma proteins associated with breast cancer risk, including ancestry-and subtype-differentiated signals, and prioritized a subset with greater cumulative support from colocalization, external MR, and protein PGS analyses.

These findings provide a genetically informed basis for mechanistic and translational follow-up, and motivate the larger, ancestrally diverse pQTL resources needed for equitable target and biomarker discovery.

We first conducted a proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) study to evaluate associations between genetically predicted plasma protein levels and breast cancer risk.

Genetic instruments derived from European-ancestry participants in the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP; n = 34,557) were integrated with breast cancer genome-wide association studies (GWAS) from European-, East Asian-, and Africanancestry populations (156,901 cases and 204,634 controls).
Fixed-effects meta-analysis combining cross-ancestry MR estimates identified 12 candidate proteins associated with breast cancer risk.

These candidates were further evaluated using subtype-specific and reverse-direction MR analyses, statistical colocalization, external MR replication in two independent proteomic datasets (deCODE, n = 35,559; Japan COVID-19 Task Force [JCTF], n = 1,384), and phenotype-linked genetic validation in the ancestrally diverse All of Us cohort (n = 224,107).
Support varied across candidates, with a subset showing stronger multi-layer evidence.
